name: System Design Interview Prep
subject: system-design
description: Scalability, databases, caching, load balancing, and distributed systems fundamentals

questions.question: What is the purpose of a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
options: To process server-side logic closer to users
To cache and serve static assets from geographically distributed edge servers close to users
To balance database load across regions
To manage DNS records globally
questions.explanation: CDNs cache static content (images, JS, CSS) at edge nodes close to users, reducing latency and origin server load.

questions.question: What is the CAP theorem?
options: A distributed system can guarantee all of: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance simultaneously
A distributed system can guarantee at most two of: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance
A distributed system must always choose Consistency over Availability
A system's capacity follows Consistency, Availability, and Performance tradeoffs
questions.explanation: CAP theorem: in a distributed system experiencing a network partition, you must choose between Consistency (all nodes see same data) or Availability (system always responds).

questions.question: What is horizontal sharding in databases?
options: Splitting a table into separate columns across databases
Distributing rows of a table across multiple database servers by a shard key
Replicating data to read replicas
Creating separate schemas per user
questions.explanation: Sharding splits table rows across database servers by a shard key (e.g., user_id % num_shards), enabling horizontal scaling.

questions.question: What is the primary use case for a message queue (e.g., Kafka, RabbitMQ)?
options: Storing relational data
Decoupling services, enabling async communication, and buffering spikes in traffic
Serving static content to clients
Caching database query results
questions.explanation: Message queues decouple producers from consumers, absorb traffic spikes, and enable reliable async processing without tight service coupling.

questions.question: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
options: SQL is for small data; NoSQL is for big data
SQL enforces a fixed schema with ACID transactions; NoSQL trades schema flexibility and horizontal scaling for weaker consistency guarantees
NoSQL cannot store structured data
SQL databases cannot scale at all
questions.explanation: SQL: structured schema, ACID, strong consistency, vertical scaling. NoSQL: flexible schema, eventual consistency, horizontal scaling. Neither is universally better.

questions.question: What is Redis most commonly used for in a web architecture?
options: Primary relational database
In-memory caching, session storage, and pub/sub messaging
Full-text search engine
Blob storage for images
questions.explanation: Redis is an in-memory key-value store: ideal for caching (sub-millisecond reads), session storage, rate limiting, and pub/sub.

questions.question: What is a load balancer's primary function?
options: Encrypts all incoming traffic
Distributes incoming requests across multiple server instances to ensure no single server is overwhelmed
Stores session data for logged-in users
Manages DNS resolution
questions.explanation: A load balancer routes requests to healthy backend servers using algorithms like round-robin, least-connections, or IP hash.

questions.question: What is database read replication?
options: Splitting a database's tables across servers
Creating read-only copies of the primary database to serve read traffic and reduce primary load
Backing up the database to a cold storage
Compressing database indices for faster reads
questions.explanation: Read replicas receive changes from the primary (via replication log) and serve read queries, offloading the primary and improving read scalability.

questions.question: What is an API Gateway responsible for in a microservices architecture?
options: Stores API documentation
Acts as a single entry point for clients, handling routing, auth, rate limiting, and protocol translation
Manages database migrations
Provides service-to-service discovery
questions.explanation: An API Gateway is the front door: it routes requests to the right microservice, enforces auth/rate limiting, and abstracts backend complexity from clients.

questions.question: What does 'eventual consistency' mean in distributed systems?
options: Data is always consistent across all nodes instantly
Given enough time with no new updates, all nodes will converge to the same data value
Consistency is sacrificed permanently for availability
Only two out of three nodes need to agree on a value
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency: writes propagate asynchronously; nodes may temporarily disagree, but will converge to the same state if no new writes arrive.

questions.question: What is the difference between latency and throughput?
options: They are the same metric
Latency is the time to complete one request; throughput is the number of requests processed per unit time
Throughput measures data size; latency measures request count
Latency is a server metric; throughput is a client metric
questions.explanation: Latency: how long one request takes (e.g., 50ms). Throughput: how many requests are handled per second (e.g., 1000 RPS). Both are needed to characterize system performance.

questions.question: What is a circuit breaker pattern in microservices?
options: A deployment pattern that cuts production traffic during updates
A resilience pattern that stops calling a failing service and returns fallback responses to prevent cascading failures
A security pattern that blocks suspicious requests
A pattern for breaking large services into smaller ones
questions.explanation: Circuit breaker: after N failures, 'open' the circuit (stop calling the service) and return a fallback. Prevents downstream failures from cascading.

questions.question: What is consistent hashing used for?
options: Ensuring data integrity with cryptographic hashes
Distributing keys across cache/database nodes in a way that minimizes remapping when nodes are added or removed
Hashing passwords consistently across services
Balancing request load using hash values
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing maps keys to a ring; adding/removing nodes only remaps a fraction of keys (vs. modulo hashing which remaps most keys).

questions.question: What is the role of a write-ahead log (WAL) in a database?
options: Logs all user queries for analytics
Ensures durability by recording changes to a log before applying them, enabling crash recovery
Writes data to disk faster by batching operations
Provides a history of schema changes
questions.explanation: WAL writes intent before modifying data on disk. On crash recovery, the WAL is replayed to restore committed transactions and undo incomplete ones.

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem in applications using an ORM?
options: Running N+1 database instances for redundancy
Executing 1 query to fetch N parent records, then N separate queries to fetch each parent's related records
A query that returns N+1 more rows than expected
Joining N+1 tables in a single query
questions.explanation: N+1: fetch 100 users (1 query), then for each user fetch their orders (100 queries) = 101 queries. Fix with eager loading (JOIN or batch fetch).
